newsitem.title: USA: NYC should boost small businesses - PaineWebber CEO.
newsitem.headline: NYC should boost small businesses - PaineWebber CEO.

text.p: New York City, whose economic recovery though strong still lags the nation, should do more to strengthen small business if it wants to turn that picture around, the chairman of PaineWebber Group said Tuesday.

Donald Marron, who also serves as the brokerage's chief executive officer, said one of the main constraints for his business was the lack of skilled money managers, as their numbers are not keeping up with the growth of assests.
"That's usually our undoing," Marron said, referring to the brokerage industry as a whole. He made the remarks at a business breakfast sponsored by Crain's New York Business.
Individual investors now direct more of their investments because defined contribution plans, like 401 (K) savings plans, have started taking over from defined benefit plans.
Noting he got his start on Wall Street by starting and running small firms, Marron, said such companies were a good source for talented professionals.
While the Giuliani Administration's success in combatting crime has aided recruitment, Marron said prospective employees now fret about finding affordable housing.
He also focused on other sectors that could benefit from more attention. "Tourism has never been organized the way it should," he said.

Another panelist, Drew Nieporent, president of Myriad Restaurant Group, which owns a number of restaurants, primarily in TriBecca, said his businesses thrived in part because they attracted tourists, eager to explore downtown Manhattan. "I do see our numbers going up," he said, explaining that much of the new growth appeared to stem from a willingness to drink more expensive wines, as his customers sometimes resisted paying more for food.

"In general, I think New York has a bright future in terms of the restaurant business," he said later, citing the recent popularity of French bistros. But Nieporent noted the business was highly competitive, adding profit margins were thin. He predicted a number of recently opened restaurants would fail over the next few years.

New York City also needs to direct more of its efforts to the outer boroughs, the PaineWebber executive said. "New York City is not only Manhattan," he said, noting the South Bronx has large tracts of land and waterfront that could be put to work.
"The city has to do more to encourage small business to come. It's a very tough place to break into if you're small," he concluded.

Mark Wheeler, senior executive vice president, Fleet Bank, who also addressed the group, focused on how the banks' clients, which typically are smaller companies with up to $15 million or so of revenues, viewed the economy.

Among the sectors he looked to perform well over the near-term, he listed business services, which has benefited from Wall Street's boom, healthcare, which still needs capital to grow and make new alliances, tourism and entertainment, and the apparel industry, which has undergone a shake-out that has left surviving firms stronger.

Silicon Alley, a section of downtown Manhattan known for software programmers who specialize in helping media and advertizing firms grow via the Internet, for example, was seen as a turbulent but growing area that could get a boost from a rise immigration from Asia and Eastern Europe.
Fred Wilson, a venture capitalist and partner with Flatiron Partners, said this wave of new talent could help the city compete with California's renowned Silicon Valley.

He added: "Companies start and close everyday," noting that when they grew, these downtown firms often created well-paying jobs, while the Internet industry also was helping big firms, like accountants, grow by offering new services.
